Mock 17-01.text: The early Vedic community was a pastoral, semi‑nomadic tribe (jana) governed by clan assemblies (Sabha, Samiti). By the Mahajanapada era these tribes settled on fertile river plains, forming territorial agrarian states (janapada) with defined boundaries. Political power shifted from collective, lineage‑based councils to hereditary monarchs in most regions, while some areas (Vajji, Malla) developed oligarchic republics (gana‑sanghas). The varna system, originally occupational, became rigidly birth‑based, giving rise to numerous jatis that stratified society. The spread of iron tools (PGW/NBPW) cleared dense forests, boosted agricultural surplus and spurred a second urbanisation with towns and markets. Regular revenue systems—bhaga, bali and shulka—were instituted, and standing armies replaced the earlier voluntary tribal levies, consolidating state authority.

Mock 17-02.text: Subhas Chandra Bose radicalised the nationalist agenda by insisting on Purna Swaraj at the Haripura (1938) and Tripuri (1939) sessions and by founding the Forward Bloc, signalling an uncompromising demand for complete independence. He reorganised the Azad Hind Fauj in Southeast Asia in 1943, establishing the Provisional Government of Free India (Arzi Hukumat‑e‑Azad Hind) to give the movement a sovereign face. The INA mobilised Indians across religion, caste, the diaspora and women, exemplified by the Rani of Jhansi Regiment under Capt. Lakshmi Swaminathan. Its military thrust on the Indo‑Burma front – the Imphal‑Kohima battles and the flag‑hoisting at Moirang – internationalised the struggle. The 1945‑46 Red Fort INA trials sparked a mass upsurge, eroding British loyalty in the armed forces and prompting the RIN mutiny of 1946.
